topics.t: Belgium: sharing power to stay together
topics.h: How does a country where people speak three languages avoid a fight over who is in charge? Belgium found a clever answer!
p: Belgium is a small European country (smaller in area than Haryana) bordering the Netherlands, France, Germany and Luxembourg.
Its people: about 59% live in the Flemish region and speak Dutch, about 40% live in the Wallonia region and speak French, and about 1% speak German.

In the capital Brussels the picture flips: about 80% speak French and only 20% speak Dutch. The French-speaking minority was richer and more powerful, which the Dutch speakers resented, and tensions rose in the 1950s and 1960s.
Between 1970 and 1993 Belgium amended its Constitution four times so that everyone could live together. The country became federal in 1993.

The Belgian model: an equal number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers in the central government; powerful state governments not under the Centre; a separate Brussels government with equal representation; and a 'community government' for each language group dealing with culture, education and language.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the French speakers of Brussels agree to share power equally there, even though they were the majority in the city?
st: In Brussels, French speakers were the majority (80%).
In the country as a whole, Dutch speakers were the majority (59%) yet accepted equal representation in the central government.
Each side gave up something where it was strong, so that it would be treated fairly where it was weak.
ex.a: It was a two-way deal: French speakers accepted equality in Brussels because Dutch speakers accepted equality in the central government.

topics.rl: Brussels is also the headquarters of the European Union. Think of a class monitor team where one monitor is chosen from each section so that no section feels left out — that is the Belgian idea in miniature.

topics.t: Sri Lanka: the danger of majoritarianism
topics.h: Two neighbours with different languages: one chose to share, the other chose to rule alone. Sri Lanka shows what happens with the second choice.
p: Sri Lanka is an island nation a few kilometres off the southern coast of Tamil Nadu. It became independent in 1948.

About 74% of the people speak Sinhala and about 18% speak Tamil. Among Tamils, Sri Lankan Tamils are about 13%; the rest are Indian Tamils, whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers in colonial times. Sri Lankan Tamils live mostly in the north and east.
Most Sinhala speakers are Buddhists; most Tamils are Hindus or Muslims; about 7% of people are Christians, who are both Tamil and Sinhala.

Majoritarian measures: a 1956 Act made Sinhala the only official language; Sinhala applicants were preferred for university positions and government jobs; and the Constitution said the state shall protect and foster Buddhism.

Sri Lankan Tamils felt alienated. They demanded Tamil as an official language, regional autonomy and equal opportunity. By the 1980s some groups demanded an independent Tamil Eelam in the north and east, and a long civil war followed, which ended in 2009.

ex.q: Think it through: The Sinhala community was the majority. Why did ruling only in its own interest not bring peace?
st: Majoritarianism means the majority rules as it wishes, ignoring the needs of the minority.
Tamils were denied an equal share in language, jobs and education, so they felt the government was not theirs.
When a group feels permanently left out, trust breaks down; in Sri Lanka this led to conflict and a civil war.
ex.a: Ignoring the minority undermined the unity of the country; majoritarian rule weakened, rather than strengthened, Sri Lanka.

topics.rl: Imagine a school picnic where only the biggest group decides the food, games and timing every year. Soon the rest stop coming. Including everyone keeps the group together.

topics.t: Why share power, and the forms of power sharing
topics.h: Power sharing is like a Diwali thali: many dishes on one plate, each with its own place. Why share, and how?
p: Prudential reason: sharing power reduces the chance of conflict between social groups and ensures political stability. It is wise in the long run.
Moral reason: sharing power is the very spirit of democracy. People affected by decisions have a right to be consulted and to live under a government they accept as legitimate.
Horizontal sharing: power is shared among organs of government at the same level — legislature, executive and judiciary. Each checks the others: a system of checks and balances.

Vertical sharing: power is shared among governments at different levels — a general government for the whole country and governments at the state or provincial level, and below them local governments such as panchayats and municipalities. This is federal division of power.

Power is also shared among social groups (like Belgium's community government, or reserved constituencies in India) and among political parties, pressure groups and movements (competition among parties, coalition governments, and interest groups influencing decisions).

ex.q: Think it through: The Supreme Court strikes down a law passed by Parliament. Which form of power sharing is this?
st: Parliament (legislature) and the Supreme Court (judiciary) are organs of government at the same level.
One organ is checking another, so no organ has unlimited power.
Sharing among organs at the same level is horizontal power sharing.
ex.a: Horizontal power sharing — an example of checks and balances.

topics.rl: Your housing society has an elected committee, a treasurer who keeps accounts and an auditor who checks them. No one person can do everything — that is checks and balances in daily life.

topics.h: One country, many governments, the same citizens — and yet no chaos. How? Welcome to federalism!
p: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and its various constituent units (like states or provinces).

In a unitary system there is only one level of government, or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government, which can pass orders to them. Sri Lanka remains a unitary system, while Belgium became federal in 1993.

Key features: (1) two or more levels (tiers) of government; (2) each tier governs the same citizens but has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration; (3) these jurisdictions are written in the constitution, so each tier's existence and authority are constitutionally guaranteed.

(4) Fundamental provisions of the constitution cannot be changed by one level alone — both levels must agree; (5) courts interpret the constitution and the powers of each level, and the highest court acts as umpire in disputes; (6) sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified.
Dual objective: to safeguard and promote the unity of the country, and at the same time to accommodate regional diversity. Mutual trust and agreement to live together are needed for it to work.

ex.q: Think it through: In Country X, the national government can dissolve a province's government whenever it likes and take away its powers by a simple order. Is Country X federal?
st: In a federation, each level's powers are guaranteed by the constitution.
One level cannot alone change or take away the powers of the other.
Here the provinces depend entirely on the national government's orders, so they are subordinate.
ex.a: No. Country X is unitary in practice, because its provinces are subordinate to the Centre.

topics.rl: Your school has a principal for the whole school and a class teacher for each class. Both guide the same students, but each has fixed duties — a little like levels in a federation.

topics.h: India's Constitution never uses the word 'federation' — yet India is federal. Let's find the proof!
p: Coming together federations: independent states come together to form a bigger unit, and the units usually have equal power (USA, Switzerland, Australia). Holding together federations: a large country divides power between the Centre and the states; the Centre tends to be stronger and units may have unequal powers (India, Spain, Belgium).
The Constitution declared India a Union of States. Originally there were two tiers — Union and states; later a third tier of panchayats and municipalities was added.

Three lists: Union List (national importance: defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications, currency); State List (local importance: police, trade, commerce, agriculture, irrigation); Concurrent List (both: education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption, succession). If laws conflict on a Concurrent subject, the Union law prevails.

Residuary subjects (not in any list, like computer software) are for the Union government. Union Territories, such as Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi, do not have the powers of a state; the Central government has special powers in running them.

Changing the power-sharing arrangement is not easy: an amendment must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states. The judiciary (High Courts and Supreme Court) settles disputes over division of powers.

ex.q: Think it through: A law on 'computer software' is needed. It is not in any of the three lists. Who can make it?
st: Subjects not mentioned in any list are called residuary subjects.
The Constitution gives the Union government power to legislate on residuary subjects.
Computer software came up after the Constitution was made, so it is residuary.
ex.a: The Union government (Parliament) can make the law.

topics.rl: Your local police station is run by the state government, while your passport is issued by the Union government — that is the Union and State Lists at work.

topics.t: How federalism is practised in India
topics.h: A good constitution is a recipe — but the taste depends on how it is cooked. How has India actually practised federalism?
p: Linguistic states: after 1947 the boundaries of many old states were changed and new states created so that people speaking the same language lived in the same state. Some states were formed on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography, like Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand.
Some leaders feared linguistic states would lead to disintegration, but experience shows they made the country more united and administration easier.

Language policy: our Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language. Hindi was identified as the official language, but it is the mother tongue of only about 40% of Indians. Besides Hindi, 21 other languages are recognised as Scheduled Languages (22 in all).

English was to stop being used for official purposes in 1965, but many non-Hindi-speaking states demanded that it continue. The Central government agreed to continue English along with Hindi for official purposes.

Centre-state relations: for a long time the same party ruled at the Centre and in most states, and the Centre sometimes misused the Constitution to dismiss state governments. After 1990, regional parties grew and coalition governments at the Centre became common, building a culture of power sharing and respect for state autonomy. A Supreme Court judgment also made it difficult to dismiss state governments arbitrarily.

ex.q: Think it through: Why did the Central government not force Hindi on non-Hindi-speaking states?
st: India has great linguistic diversity; Hindi is the mother tongue of only about 40% of people.
Imposing one language could have alienated other language groups, as happened in Sri Lanka.
A flexible, accommodating policy kept trust between the Centre and the states.
ex.a: Because accommodating all languages strengthens unity, while imposing one could have caused conflict.

topics.rl: A candidate can write the exam for a Central government job in any of the Scheduled Languages — a real sign of India's respect for language diversity.

topics.h: Who knows best where your village needs a new handpump? Not someone far away in the state capital — but people right there!
p: Decentralisation means taking power away from the Central and state governments and giving it to local government. The basic idea: many problems are best settled locally, and people can participate directly in decisions.
A major step came in 1992, when the Constitution was amended to make the third tier more powerful and effective.

Key provisions: regular elections to local bodies are compulsory; seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes; at least one-third of all positions are reserved for women; each state has a State Election Commission to conduct panchayat and municipal elections; state governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.

Rural local government (panchayati raj): a gram panchayat has ward members (panch) and a president (sarpanch), elected by the adult population, and works under the gram sabha (all the voters of the village). Panchayats are grouped into a panchayat samiti (block or mandal), and all panchayat samitis in a district form the zilla parishad, whose chairperson is its political head.

Urban local government: municipalities in towns and municipal corporations in big cities. The municipal chairperson heads a municipality; the mayor heads a municipal corporation. Challenges remain: gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most states have not given significant powers and resources to local bodies.

ex.q: Think it through: A gram panchayat wants to repair the village pond. Who must approve its annual budget and review its work?
st: The gram panchayat works under the overall supervision of the gram sabha.
The gram sabha consists of all the voters of the village.
It meets at least twice or thrice a year to approve the budget and review the panchayat's performance.
ex.a: The gram sabha — all the voters of the village.

topics.rl: When your town elects ward councillors and your city has a mayor, or your grandparents' village elects a sarpanch, you are seeing decentralisation.

topics.t: Gender division and women in politics
topics.h: Who makes the chai at home and who fixes the tap? Many families have unwritten rules — and those rules shape politics too.
p: Gender division is a hierarchical social division based on social expectations and stereotypes, not on biology.

Sexual division of labour: a system in which all work inside the home is done by women of the family, or organised by them through domestic helpers. Women's work at home is often unpaid and not valued, even though many women also work outside.

Women around the world organised and agitated for equal rights — first for the right to vote, then for equal opportunities in education, work and political life. More radical movements that aim at equality in personal and family life too are called feminist movements. In Sweden, Norway and Finland, women's participation in public life is very high.

Patriarchy (literally 'rule by father') is a system that values men more and gives them power over women. In India, problems include lower literacy among women, unequal pay despite the law of equal wages for equal work, a preference for sons that has lowered the child sex ratio, and unsafe public spaces.

Political representation: at least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women. Women's share in Parliament and state assemblies has been low. The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) reserves about one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, the state legislative assemblies and the Delhi Assembly for women. It takes effect only after the next census and a fresh delimitation of constituencies, so these seats are not reserved yet. Exam tip: older printings of the NCERT book describe this as a bill still pending in Parliament; answer using the wording in your own copy of the textbook.

ex.q: Think it through: Why does it matter if very few women sit in the legislature, even though women can vote?
st: Legislatures make the laws and policies that affect everyone.
If women are poorly represented, issues like safety, equal pay and health may get less attention.
Reserving seats is one way to make sure women's voices are heard where decisions are made.
ex.a: Because representation affects which problems get solved; more women in legislatures helps bring women's concerns into policy.

topics.rl: Notice how many women sarpanches and councillors now lead villages and towns across India — the one-third reservation in local bodies has made that possible.

topics.t: Religion, communalism and the secular state
topics.h: India is home to many faiths — Diwali lamps, Eid sweets, Christmas stars and Gurpurab langars. How does democracy keep this harmony?
p: Religion and politics: Gandhiji said religion can never be separated from politics — by religion he meant the moral values common to all religions, not any one faith. People may express their needs and interests in politics as members of a religious community.

Communalism is the problem: when one religion's beliefs are presented as superior, when the demands of one religious group are formed in opposition to another, and when state power is used to establish the domination of one religious group.

Forms of communalism: everyday beliefs and stereotypes about other religions; a desire for political dominance of one's own community (or a separate political unit); political mobilisation on religious lines using sacred symbols and emotional appeals; and, at its ugliest, communal violence. India saw terrible communal violence at the time of Partition.

India is a secular state: there is no official religion (unlike Sri Lanka, whose constitution gives a special place to Buddhism); everyone is free to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not follow any; and discrimination on grounds of religion is prohibited.
The Constitution also allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities — for example, it bans untouchability.

ex.q: Think it through: A leader tells voters, 'Vote only for people of your own religion, because the other community is against you.' Is this communalism?
st: The message presents one religious group's interests as opposed to another's.
It uses religious identity to mobilise votes and spreads distrust.
Expressing needs as a community is allowed; setting communities against each other is communalism.
ex.a: Yes. It is communal politics, because it builds hostility between religious groups for political gain.

topics.rl: When your school celebrates Holi, Eid, Christmas and Guru Nanak Jayanti together, it reflects the spirit of a secular state that treats all faiths with equal respect.

topics.h: Caste can shape politics, and politics can reshape caste. It's a two-way street!
p: Caste division is special to India: occupations were passed down hereditarily, people married within their caste, and some groups faced exclusion and untouchability.

Social reformers such as Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker worked for a society without caste inequality. Urbanisation, literacy, education and occupational mobility have weakened old caste rules, and the Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination.

Caste in politics: parties consider the caste composition of voters when choosing candidates; parties and candidates may appeal to caste sentiment; universal adult franchise made leaders mobilise all groups; and it gave dalits and backward castes a sense of political voice.

But elections are not only about caste: no parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste; no party wins all the votes of a caste; many voters have no candidate from their caste; and ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose. Voters also judge performance, leaders and party policies.

Politics in caste: each caste group tries to grow by including neighbouring castes, forms coalitions with others, and new groupings like 'backward' and 'forward' castes emerge. Caste still links with economic status: on average upper castes are better off, while dalits and adivasis are worse off.

ex.q: Think it through: A party picks a candidate of the largest caste in a constituency. Is it sure to win?
st: No constituency has a clear majority of one caste, so one caste alone cannot decide the result.
No party gets all the votes of any one caste.
Voters also weigh the government's work, the leaders and the parties' policies.
ex.a: No. Caste matters, but no candidate can win on caste votes alone.

topics.rl: In any election season, you can read news about parties discussing which communities live in a constituency — and also about the issues voters care about, like roads, water and jobs.

topics.t: What parties are and what they do
topics.h: Imagine an election with 500 independent candidates and no parties. Who would form the government? Who would be responsible? Parties solve this puzzle.
p: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for society, aiming at the collective good.
A party has three components: leaders, active members, and followers (supporters). Since a party is a part of society, it involves partisanship — taking a side on issues.

Functions of parties: (1) contest elections — in most democracies candidates are put up by parties; (2) put forward different policies and programmes for voters to choose from; (3) play a decisive role in making laws; (4) form and run governments; (5) those that lose play the role of opposition, criticising the government and mobilising people.

(6) Shape public opinion by raising and highlighting issues; (7) provide people access to government machinery and welfare schemes — local party leaders are easier to approach than government officers.

Why we need parties: without them every candidate would be independent, no one could promise major policy changes, and no one would be responsible for running the country. Parties grew along with representative democracies.

ex.q: Think it through: In the USA, members and supporters of a party choose its candidates. How is this different in India?
st: In some countries, such as the USA, party members and supporters select candidates.
In India, top party leaders usually choose the candidates.
Both are ways of carrying out the first function of parties — contesting elections.
ex.a: In India top party leaders choose the candidates, while in the USA members and supporters do.

topics.rl: Before elections, parties release manifestos listing their promises on jobs, farming, schools and health — that is the 'policies and programmes' function at work.

topics.t: Party systems: one, two or many
topics.h: Some countries are like a one-team match, some like India vs Australia, and some like the IPL with many teams. Which party system fits where?
p: One-party system: only one party is allowed to control and run the government. In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule. This is not a democratic option, because voters have no real choice.
Two-party system: power usually changes between two main parties. Other parties exist but rarely win enough seats. The United States of America and the United Kingdom are examples.
Multiparty system: several parties compete for power, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power, either on their own or in alliance. India has a multiparty system.

When several parties come together to contest elections and win power, the group is called an alliance or a front. A multiparty system can look messy and may lead to political instability, but it allows a variety of interests and opinions to be represented.

No party system is ideal for all countries. A party system is not chosen by a country; it evolves over a long time depending on the nature of society, its social and regional divisions, its history and its system of elections.

ex.q: Think it through: Why has India ended up with a multiparty system rather than a two-party system?
st: India is very large and has great social and geographical diversity.
Different regions and groups have their own concerns and want them represented.
Two parties cannot easily absorb all this diversity, so many parties emerged.
ex.a: Because India's size and social and regional diversity are better reflected by many parties.

topics.rl: During elections you see many party symbols on the EVM — from national parties to state parties — a living picture of India's multiparty system.

topics.h: Every party symbol on the ballot has a story. Which parties get a fixed symbol, and how do they become national or state parties?
p: Every party in India has to register with the Election Commission. The Commission treats all parties equally but gives some special facilities to large, established parties.
Parties given these facilities are called 'recognised' parties. A recognised party gets a unique election symbol, which only its official candidates can use.
State party (as per the textbook): a party that secures at least 6% of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a state and wins at least two seats.

National party (as per the textbook): a party that secures at least 6% of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or in Assembly elections in four states, and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha.

State parties are often called 'regional parties', but they need not be regional in ideology. Over time, state parties have become stronger, and since 1996 nearly every state party has had a chance to be part of a national-level coalition government, strengthening federalism.

ex.q: Think it through: Party P gets 7% of the votes in a state Assembly election and wins three seats. Does it qualify as a state party?
st: The textbook rule needs at least 6% of the total votes in the Assembly election.
It also needs at least two seats.
7% is more than 6%, and three seats are more than two.
ex.a: Yes. Party P meets both conditions, so it can be recognised as a state party.

topics.rl: Look at the ballot paper or EVM list in your area: recognised parties appear with their fixed symbols, while many independents get symbols from a free list.

topics.t: Challenges to parties and how to reform them
topics.h: Parties are the engine of democracy — but even a great engine needs servicing. What goes wrong, and how can we fix it?
p: Challenge 1 — lack of internal democracy: power gets concentrated in a few top leaders; parties do not keep membership registers, hold organisational meetings or conduct internal elections regularly.

Challenge 2 — dynastic succession: top positions often go to members of one family, which is unfair to other members. Challenge 3 — growing role of money and muscle power, especially during elections. Challenge 4 — lack of meaningful choice, as differences in the policies of parties have reduced.

Reforms already made: the Constitution was amended to stop elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties (anti-defection law) — a member who changes party loses the seat. The Supreme Court made it mandatory for every candidate to file an affidavit giving details of property and pending criminal cases. The Election Commission made it necessary for parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns.

Suggested reforms: a law to regulate the internal affairs of parties; making it compulsory to give about one-third of tickets to women candidates; and state funding of elections, where the government gives parties money to support their election expenses.
Pressure from citizens matters too: people can press parties through petitions, publicity and agitations, and those who want reform can themselves join political parties.

ex.q: Think it through: How does a candidate's affidavit help voters?
st: The affidavit lists the candidate's property and any criminal cases pending against them.
This information is made public before voting.
Voters can use it to make a more informed choice.
ex.a: It gives voters information about a candidate's assets and criminal cases so they can choose wisely.

topics.rl: Before elections, news channels and websites often publish summaries of candidates' affidavits — that is this reform in action.

topics.h: Democracy is like a school report card: we judge it by its results. What should we expect, and how do we measure it?
p: Democracy is preferred because it promotes equality among citizens, enhances the dignity of the individual, improves the quality of decision-making, provides a method to resolve conflicts, and allows room to correct mistakes.
Democracy only creates conditions for achieving goals; citizens must use those conditions. Its outcomes should be judged against realistic expectations.

An accountable government: citizens have the right and the means to examine the process of decision-making. This is called transparency. Democracy ensures decisions are taken according to rules and procedures.
Decisions in a democracy may be slower because of discussion and negotiation, but they are more acceptable to people and more effective. The cost of time is worth it.

A democratic government is a legitimate government — it may be slow, less efficient or not always responsive, but it is the people's own government. Regular, free and fair elections, open public debate and citizens' right to information help keep it accountable and responsive.

ex.q: Think it through: A dictator builds a road in one month; a democratic government takes six months after public meetings. Which decision is better in the long run?
st: The dictator's decision is quick, but people had no say and may not accept it.
The democratic process is slow, but people were consulted, so the decision is more acceptable.
Acceptable decisions are carried out more effectively and are less likely to cause conflict.
ex.a: The democratic decision is often better in the long run because it is more acceptable and effective, even if slower.

topics.rl: Under the Right to Information, any citizen can ask a government office for information about how a decision was made — a tool of transparency.

topics.h: If democracy is the people's government, will it make everyone rich and equal? The honest answer is: not automatically.
p: Studies show dictatorships have had a slightly higher rate of economic growth than democracies, but the difference is negligible. Democracy cannot simply be blamed for slow growth.
Economic development depends on several factors: the country's population size, the global situation, cooperation from other countries and the economic priorities adopted by the country.
Even if growth is slightly lower, democracy is preferable because it has many other positive outcomes like dignity, accountability and freedom.

Democracies are based on political equality — every adult citizen has one vote with equal value. Yet economic inequality remains: a small number of ultra-rich people enjoy a large share of wealth and income, while those at the bottom have very little.

Since the poor are a large part of the voters, one might expect democracies to focus on reducing poverty. But democracies do not appear to be very successful in reducing economic inequalities, and in many countries people still lack basic needs.

ex.q: Think it through: Every citizen has one vote of equal value. Why does economic inequality still continue in democracies?
st: Political equality (one person, one vote) is not the same as economic equality.
Many factors beyond voting decide incomes, such as growth, opportunities and government priorities.
So equal votes do not automatically produce equal incomes.
ex.a: Because political equality does not by itself guarantee economic equality.

topics.rl: Every voter in a city — whether living in a big bungalow or a small rented room — gets one vote of equal value on election day, yet their incomes may be very different.

topics.t: Social diversity, dignity and freedom of citizens
topics.h: A good democracy is like a big family get-together: different tastes, different opinions, but everyone gets a seat at the table.
p: Democracies usually develop a procedure to conduct their competition peacefully, which reduces the chance of tensions turning violent. Belgium is a good example of successfully negotiating differences among groups.

Two conditions are needed: majority and minority opinions must work together (democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion), and rule by majority must not become rule by the majority community in terms of religion, race or language. Anyone should be able to be part of the majority at some point.
Dignity and freedom: democracy is far better than any other form of government in promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual. Every person wants respect from others.

Dignity of women: in most societies women were long treated as unequal. Democracy accepts in principle that women are equal, legally and morally, so their struggle for equal treatment now has support.

Caste: democracy has strengthened the claims of disadvantaged and discriminated castes for equal status and equal opportunity. Expectations from democracy keep rising, and people complaining about it is itself proof of its success — they have become aware and able to judge the government critically.

ex.q: Think it through: People in a democracy complain loudly about their government. Is this a sign of failure?
st: Complaining shows people expect a lot and are aware of their rights.
They feel free to look critically at those in power.
People who were once subjects have become citizens who judge their rulers.
ex.a: No. The fact that people complain is itself a testimony to the success of democracy.

topics.rl: When a woman sarpanch leads a gram sabha in Rajasthan or a first-generation student becomes an IAS officer, you see democracy widening dignity and opportunity.

qa.q: Which language is spoken by the majority of people in Belgium as a whole?
qa.a: Dutch
qa.e: About 59% of Belgians live in the Flemish region and speak Dutch.

qa.q: In the city of Brussels, what share of people speak French?
qa.a: About 80%
qa.e: In Brussels about 80% speak French and 20% speak Dutch, the reverse of the national picture.

qa.q: How many times did Belgium amend its Constitution between 1970 and 1993?
qa.e: Belgian leaders amended the Constitution four times in this period to build an arrangement where all communities could live together.

qa.q: What subjects does the 'community government' in Belgium deal with?
qa.a: Cultural, educational and language-related issues
qa.e: The community government is elected by one language community and looks after culture, education and language.

qa.q: Why did Dutch-speaking people resent the French-speaking community before the changes?
qa.a: The French speakers were relatively rich and powerful even though they were a minority in the country
qa.e: The French-speaking minority was richer and more powerful; Dutch speakers got the benefits of economic development and education much later.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT part of the Belgian model of power sharing?
qa.a: Declaring Dutch as the only official language because Dutch speakers are the majority
qa.e: Belgium avoided majority rule by one community; making one language the only official language is what Sri Lanka did, not Belgium.

qa.q: Some special laws in Belgium need the support of a majority of members from each linguistic group. What does this achieve?
qa.a: No single community can take decisions on its own
qa.e: Requiring a majority from each group means both communities must agree, so neither can impose its will on the other.

qa.q: In which year did Belgium shift from a unitary to a federal form of government?
qa.e: The last of the four constitutional amendments (1970-1993) came in 1993, when Belgium became federal.

qa.q: In which year did Sri Lanka become an independent country?
qa.e: Sri Lanka gained independence in 1948.

qa.q: What did the 1956 Act in Sri Lanka do?
qa.a: Recognised Sinhala as the only official language
qa.e: The 1956 Act recognised Sinhala as the only official language, disregarding Tamil.

qa.q: What is 'majoritarianism'?
qa.a: The belief that the majority community should rule in whichever way it wants, disregarding the minority
qa.e: Majoritarianism ignores the wishes and needs of the minority; it is the opposite of power sharing.

qa.q: About what percentage of Sri Lanka's people speak Sinhala?
qa.e: Sinhala speakers are about 74% and Tamil speakers about 18% of the population.

qa.q: Who are the 'Indian Tamils' of Sri Lanka?
qa.a: Tamils whose forefathers came from India as plantation workers in colonial times
qa.e: Indian Tamils are Sri Lankan citizens whose ancestors were brought from India to work on plantations during colonial rule.

qa.q: Which was NOT a demand of the Sri Lankan Tamil political parties?
qa.a: Making Buddhism the state religion
qa.e: Protecting and fostering Buddhism was a majoritarian provision of the government; Tamil parties demanded language recognition, autonomy and equal opportunity.

qa.q: Where were the Sri Lankan Tamils mainly concentrated?
qa.a: North and east of the country
qa.e: Sri Lankan Tamils lived mainly in the north and east, which is why the demand for Tamil Eelam was for that area.

qa.q: What is the main lesson from comparing Belgium and Sri Lanka?
qa.a: Power sharing keeps a country united, while majoritarianism can break it apart
qa.e: Belgium accommodated its communities and stayed united; Sri Lanka's majoritarian policies led to distrust and civil war.

qa.q: Which statement is a PRUDENTIAL reason for power sharing?
qa.a: Power sharing reduces conflict between social groups and brings political stability
qa.e: Prudential reasons are about good outcomes — less conflict and more stability.

qa.q: Which statement is a MORAL reason for power sharing?
qa.a: It is the very spirit of democracy, since citizens have a right to be consulted
qa.e: The moral reason values power sharing for its own sake: in a democracy, those affected by power should share in it.

qa.q: Power shared among the legislature, executive and judiciary is called:
qa.a: Horizontal distribution of power
qa.e: These organs are at the same level, so sharing among them is horizontal.

qa.q: Which is an example of vertical division of power in India?
qa.a: Separate powers for the Union government, state governments and panchayats
qa.e: Vertical division shares power among levels of government — Union, state and local.

qa.q: Reserved constituencies in assemblies and Parliament in India are an example of power sharing among:
qa.a: Social groups
qa.e: Reserved constituencies give socially weaker sections a share in power, which is sharing among social groups.

qa.q: What is meant by 'checks and balances'?
qa.a: Each organ of government checks the others, so no organ has unlimited power
qa.e: Under checks and balances, legislature, executive and judiciary keep each other within limits.

qa.q: When two or more political parties join hands to form a government, it is called:
qa.a: A coalition government
qa.e: A coalition government shares power among parties — one form of power sharing among political parties.

qa.q: Interest groups of traders, farmers or industrial workers influence decisions by taking part in committees or putting pressure on the government. This is power sharing among:
qa.a: Political parties, pressure groups and movements
qa.e: Pressure groups and movements also get a share in governmental power by influencing the decision-making process.

qa.q: What is federalism?
qa.a: A system where power is divided between a central authority and its constituent units
qa.e: In federalism power is divided between the Centre and units such as states or provinces.

qa.q: Which of these describes a UNITARY system?
qa.a: Sub-units are subordinate to the central government
qa.e: In a unitary system there is either one level, or the sub-units are subordinate to the Centre.

qa.q: How can the fundamental provisions of a federal constitution be changed?
qa.a: Only with the consent of both levels of government
qa.e: No single level can unilaterally change the basic provisions; both levels must agree.

qa.q: Who acts as an umpire if disputes arise between levels of government in a federation?
qa.a: The highest court
qa.e: Courts interpret the constitution and the powers of each level; the highest court acts as umpire.

qa.q: What is the dual objective of a federal system?
qa.a: Safeguard national unity and accommodate regional diversity
qa.e: Federalism aims to keep the country united while respecting regional diversity.

qa.q: Which country shifted from a unitary to a federal form of government in 1993?
qa.a: Belgium
qa.e: Belgium became federal in 1993, while Sri Lanka remains essentially unitary.

qa.q: In a federation, each tier of government has its own jurisdiction in which matters?
qa.a: Specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration
qa.e: Each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration.

qa.q: Why are the jurisdictions of each level written in the constitution in a federation?
qa.a: So that the existence and authority of each tier are constitutionally guaranteed
qa.e: Writing them in the constitution protects each level's powers from being taken away by the other.

qa.q: India is an example of which type of federation?
qa.a: Holding together federation
qa.e: India is a large country that divided power between the Centre and the states — a holding together federation.

qa.q: Which subject is in the Union List?
qa.a: Defence
qa.e: Defence is of national importance, so it is in the Union List. Police and agriculture are State subjects; education is Concurrent.

qa.q: Education, forest and trade unions are subjects of which list?
qa.a: Concurrent List
qa.e: Both the Union and state governments can make laws on Concurrent List subjects like these.

qa.q: If a Union law and a state law conflict on a Concurrent List subject, which prevails?
qa.a: The Union law
qa.e: On Concurrent subjects, the law made by the Union government prevails in case of conflict.

qa.q: Who has the power to make laws on residuary subjects such as computer software?
qa.a: The Union government
qa.e: Residuary subjects are not in any list, and the Constitution gives power over them to the Union government.

qa.q: To change the power-sharing arrangement between the Union and states, an amendment must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority and then:
qa.a: Ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states
qa.e: Both levels must agree: Parliament with a two-thirds majority, then at least half of the state legislatures.

qa.q: Which of these is a Union Territory?
qa.a: Lakshadweep
qa.e: Lakshadweep is a Union Territory; the Central government has special powers in running it. Kerala, Punjab and Assam are states.

qa.q: Which country is an example of a 'coming together' federation?
qa.a: United States of America
qa.e: In the USA independent states came together to form a bigger unit.

qa.q: On what basis were many new states created in India after 1947?
qa.a: Language of the people
qa.e: States were reorganised so that people speaking the same language lived in the same state.

qa.q: Which of these states was created on the basis of culture, ethnicity or geography rather than language alone?
qa.a: Jharkhand
qa.e: Jharkhand, like Nagaland and Uttarakhand, was formed on such grounds. The others are Union Territories, not states.

qa.q: How many languages, including Hindi, are recognised as Scheduled Languages by the Constitution?
qa.e: Hindi plus 21 other languages make 22 Scheduled Languages.

qa.q: What status does Hindi have under the Constitution?
qa.a: Official language
qa.e: Hindi was identified as the official language; the Constitution did not give any language the status of national language.

qa.q: Why did the Central government agree to continue using English along with Hindi for official purposes?
qa.a: Many non-Hindi-speaking states demanded it
qa.e: Non-Hindi-speaking states wanted English to continue, and the Centre accommodated this demand.

qa.q: What change in Centre-state relations came after 1990?
qa.a: Regional parties grew and coalition governments built respect for state autonomy
qa.e: The rise of regional parties and coalition governments at the Centre led to a new culture of power sharing.

qa.q: What was the outcome of creating linguistic states, according to experience?
qa.a: The country became more united and administration became easier
qa.e: Fears of disintegration proved wrong; linguistic states strengthened unity.

qa.q: Before 1990, how did the Central government sometimes undermine the power of the states?
qa.a: By misusing the Constitution to dismiss state governments ruled by rival parties
qa.e: The Centre at times dismissed state governments controlled by rival parties, which went against the spirit of federalism.

qa.q: What is decentralisation?
qa.a: Taking power from the Central and state governments and giving it to local government
qa.e: Decentralisation transfers power downward to local governments like panchayats and municipalities.

qa.q: In which year was the Constitution amended to make local government more powerful?
qa.e: The 1992 amendment made the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective.

qa.q: At least what fraction of all positions in local bodies are reserved for women?
qa.a: One-third
qa.e: At least one-third of all positions in panchayats and municipalities are reserved for women.

qa.q: Who conducts panchayat and municipal elections?
qa.a: The State Election Commission
qa.e: Each state has an independent State Election Commission to conduct local body elections.

qa.q: Who is the president of a gram panchayat?
qa.a: Sarpanch
qa.e: The sarpanch is the elected president of the gram panchayat; the mayor heads a municipal corporation.

qa.q: What is a gram sabha?
qa.a: All the voters of the village
qa.e: The gram sabha consists of all voters of the village and supervises the gram panchayat.

qa.q: All the panchayat samitis in a district together form the:
qa.a: Zilla parishad
qa.e: The zilla parishad is the district-level body formed by all panchayat samitis of that district.

qa.q: Which is a real difficulty that local governments still face?
qa.a: Gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most states have not given them enough powers and resources
qa.e: Despite the 1992 amendment, many local bodies lack regular gram sabhas and adequate powers and funds.

qa.q: What is meant by the 'sexual division of labour'?
qa.a: Work inside the home is done by women, or organised by them through domestic helpers, while men mostly work outside
qa.e: It is a social system in which household work is seen as women's responsibility.

qa.q: What does 'patriarchy' literally mean?
qa.a: Rule by father
qa.e: Patriarchy literally means rule by father; it is a system that gives men power over women.

qa.q: What is the main aim of feminist movements?
qa.a: Equality for women in personal, family and public life
qa.e: Feminist movements seek equal rights and opportunities for women, not dominance over men.

qa.q: In which group of countries is women's participation in public life very high?
qa.a: Scandinavian countries such as Sweden, Norway and Finland
qa.e: In Scandinavian countries women take part in public life at very high levels.

qa.q: What share of seats in panchayats and municipalities is reserved for women?
qa.a: At least one-third
qa.e: At least one-third of the seats in local government bodies are reserved for women.

qa.q: Which is a sign that Indian women still face disadvantage despite legal protection?
qa.a: Women are often paid less than men for similar work, even though the law provides equal wages
qa.e: The law says equal wages for equal work, but in practice women are often paid less.

qa.q: Why is women's work at home often not recognised?
qa.a: Because it is usually unpaid and taken for granted
qa.e: Household work is unpaid, so it is often not counted or valued, though it is essential.

qa.q: In 2023 a constitutional amendment was passed about women's representation. What does it provide?
qa.a: Reservation of one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for women, after the next census and delimitation
qa.e: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 reserves about one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies (and the Delhi Assembly) for women. It applies only after the next census and delimitation. If your NCERT copy calls it a pending bill, use the textbook's wording in the board exam.

qa.q: What did Gandhiji mean when he said religion can never be separated from politics?
qa.a: Politics should be guided by the moral values common to all religions
qa.e: By religion Gandhiji meant ethical values from all religions, not any particular faith.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of communalism?
qa.a: Presenting the beliefs of one religion as superior to those of others
qa.e: Communalism treats one religion as superior and sets religious groups against each other.

qa.q: Which is a feature of India as a secular state?
qa.a: There is no official religion
qa.e: India has no official religion and treats all religions with equal respect.

qa.q: Why does the Constitution allow the state to intervene in religious matters in some cases?
qa.a: To ensure equality within religious communities, for example by banning untouchability
qa.e: The state may intervene to protect equality, such as by banning untouchability.

qa.q: Which country's constitution gives a special place to Buddhism, unlike India?
qa.a: Sri Lanka
qa.e: Sri Lanka's constitution says the state shall protect and foster Buddhism; India has no official religion.

qa.q: Using sacred symbols, religious leaders and emotional appeals to bring followers of one religion together in politics is called:
qa.a: Political mobilisation on religious lines
qa.e: This is one of the forms communalism takes in politics.

qa.q: Which statement about religion and politics is correct?
qa.a: People may express interests as members of a religious community, but using religion to set groups against each other is communalism
qa.e: Expressing needs as a community is acceptable; the problem is when religion becomes the basis for hostility and domination.

qa.q: Which of these is a freedom guaranteed by India's Constitution?
qa.a: Freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not to follow any
qa.e: Every citizen is free to profess, practise and propagate any religion or none.

qa.q: Which of these reformers worked to end caste inequality?
qa.a: B.R. Ambedkar
qa.e: Jotiba Phule, Gandhiji, B.R. Ambedkar and Periyar Ramaswami Naicker are among those who worked against caste discrimination.

qa.q: Which factor has helped weaken old caste rules in India?
qa.a: Urbanisation, literacy and occupational mobility
qa.e: City life, education and new kinds of jobs have broken down many old caste barriers.

qa.q: Which statement shows that elections are NOT only about caste?
qa.a: No parliamentary constituency has a clear majority of one single caste
qa.e: Since no caste is a clear majority anywhere, candidates must win the support of many groups.

qa.q: How did universal adult franchise affect caste in politics?
qa.a: It made leaders seek support from all groups and gave a political voice to groups that were once neglected
qa.e: When every adult can vote, leaders must mobilise all groups, including those that were earlier excluded.

qa.q: When a caste group includes neighbouring castes to become bigger and stronger politically, it is an example of:
qa.a: Politics in caste
qa.e: Politics changes caste groups themselves — that is 'politics in caste'.

qa.q: Why do ruling parties and sitting MPs often lose elections in India?
qa.a: Because voters also judge performance, leaders and policies
qa.e: If caste alone decided results, those in power would rarely lose; voters also weigh how well the government did.

qa.q: What does the Constitution of India say about caste-based discrimination?
qa.a: It prohibits it
qa.e: The Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination and abolished untouchability.

qa.q: Which statement about caste and economic status is correct, according to the textbook?
qa.a: On average, upper castes are better off, while dalits and adivasis are worse off
qa.e: Caste continues to be linked with economic status, though every caste has both rich and poor people.

qa.q: What is a political party?
qa.a: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government
qa.e: Parties seek to win elections and hold power so that they can carry out their policies.

qa.q: Which are the three components of a political party?
qa.a: Leaders, active members and followers
qa.e: Every party has leaders, active members and followers or supporters.

qa.q: What role do parties that lose an election play in a democracy?
qa.a: They act as the opposition and criticise the government
qa.e: The opposition voices different views, criticises the government for its failures and mobilises people.

qa.q: Who usually chooses a party's candidates in India?
qa.a: Top party leaders
qa.e: In India top party leaders generally choose candidates; in the USA party members and supporters do.

qa.q: How do parties shape public opinion?
qa.a: By raising and highlighting issues and launching movements
qa.e: Parties raise issues, and their members and supporters spread their views across society.

qa.q: Why is it often easier for a citizen to approach a local party leader than a government officer?
qa.a: Party leaders need people's support and votes, so they listen to them
qa.e: Leaders depend on public support, so they try to help people reach government machinery and welfare schemes.

qa.q: What would most likely happen in a democracy without political parties?
qa.a: Every candidate would be independent, and no one would be responsible for running the country
qa.e: Without parties, no one could promise major policy changes or take collective responsibility.

qa.q: What does 'partisanship' mean?
qa.a: Taking a side and being inclined towards a particular view
qa.e: A party is a 'part' of society, so it takes sides; this is partisanship.

qa.q: Which country has a one-party system?
qa.a: China
qa.e: In China only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.

qa.q: Why is a one-party system not considered a good democratic option?
qa.a: Voters do not get a real choice
qa.e: Democracy needs at least two parties competing so that voters can choose.

qa.q: Which pair of countries are examples of a two-party system?
qa.a: United States of America and United Kingdom
qa.e: In the USA and the UK, power usually changes between two main parties.

qa.q: India's party system is best described as:
qa.a: Multiparty
qa.e: Several parties in India compete, and more than two have a reasonable chance of coming to power.

qa.q: What is an alliance or front?
qa.a: When several parties come together to contest elections and win power
qa.e: In a multiparty system, parties often join hands as an alliance or front.

qa.q: What is one advantage of a multiparty system?
qa.a: It allows a variety of interests and opinions to enjoy political representation
qa.e: Many parties can represent many groups and views, though it may sometimes cause instability.

qa.q: How does a country get its party system?
qa.a: It evolves over a long time based on the society, its divisions, history and election system
qa.e: Party systems are not chosen; they develop from a country's society and history.

qa.q: In a two-party system, what usually happens?
qa.a: Power usually changes between two main parties, though other parties may exist
qa.e: Other parties exist, but the two main parties usually win enough seats to form the government by turn.

qa.q: With which body must every political party in India register?
qa.a: The Election Commission
qa.e: All parties have to register with the Election Commission.

qa.q: What special facility does a recognised party get?
qa.a: A unique election symbol that only its official candidates can use
qa.e: Recognised parties get a fixed symbol that only their official candidates may use.

qa.q: According to the textbook, what minimum share of votes in a state Assembly election does a party need, along with at least two seats, to be a state party?
qa.e: A state party needs at least 6% of total votes in the Assembly election and at least two seats.

qa.q: To be a national party (as per the textbook), how many Lok Sabha seats must a party win along with the vote condition?
qa.a: At least four
qa.e: A national party needs at least 6% of votes in Lok Sabha or in Assembly elections in four states, and at least four Lok Sabha seats.

qa.q: Party Q wins 8% of the votes in a state Assembly election but only one seat. Can it be recognised as a state party under the textbook rule?
qa.a: No, because it won fewer than two seats
qa.e: Both conditions must be met: at least 6% votes and at least two seats. One seat is not enough.

qa.q: Why are state parties sometimes called 'regional parties'?
qa.a: Because they are recognised on the basis of their strength in a state
qa.e: Their recognition depends on performance in a state, though their ideas need not be regional.

qa.q: How has the growing strength of state parties affected Indian democracy?
qa.a: It has made state parties part of national coalition governments, strengthening federalism
qa.e: Since 1996 nearly every state party has had a chance to be part of a national-level coalition government.

qa.q: A party wins 6% of the votes in Assembly elections in four states and also wins four Lok Sabha seats. As per the textbook rule, it qualifies as a:
qa.a: National party
qa.e: It meets both national party conditions: at least 6% votes in Assembly elections in four states and at least four Lok Sabha seats.

qa.q: What is meant by 'lack of internal democracy' in a party?
qa.a: Power is concentrated in a few leaders, and the party does not hold regular internal elections or meetings
qa.e: Without internal democracy, ordinary members have little say in decisions.

qa.q: What is 'dynastic succession'?
qa.a: Top positions going to members of one family
qa.e: In dynastic succession, family members of leaders get top posts, which is unfair to other members.

qa.q: What does the anti-defection law do?
qa.a: An elected MLA or MP who changes party loses the seat
qa.e: The Constitution was amended so that legislators who change parties lose their seat in the legislature.

qa.q: Which body ordered that candidates must file an affidavit giving details of their property and criminal cases?
qa.a: The Supreme Court
qa.e: The Supreme Court passed this order to reduce the influence of money and criminals in elections.

qa.q: Which body made it necessary for parties to hold organisational elections and file income tax returns?
qa.a: The Election Commission
qa.e: This was an order of the Election Commission.

qa.q: What is 'state funding of elections'?
qa.a: The government gives parties money to support their election expenses
qa.e: It is a suggested reform to reduce the influence of money in elections.

qa.q: Which of these is a suggested reform, not one already made?
qa.a: A law making it compulsory to give about one-third of tickets to women candidates
qa.e: Giving about one-third of party tickets to women is a suggestion; the others have already been put in place. (The 2023 women's reservation amendment reserves seats in legislatures; it does not make parties give tickets to women.)

qa.q: Which challenge refers to the reduced differences in policies among major parties?
qa.a: Lack of meaningful choice
qa.e: When parties' policies look alike, voters do not get a meaningful choice.

qa.q: What does 'transparency' mean in a democracy?
qa.a: Citizens have the right and the means to examine the process of decision-making
qa.e: Transparency lets citizens check whether decisions were taken according to proper rules and procedures.

qa.q: Why may decisions in a democracy take more time?
qa.a: Because they involve discussion, deliberation and negotiation
qa.e: Democracy is based on consultation, so it takes time, but the decisions are more acceptable.

qa.q: Which outcome can democracy be expected to produce most clearly?
qa.a: A government that is accountable to citizens and responsive to their needs
qa.e: The most basic outcome of democracy is an accountable, responsive and legitimate government.

qa.q: Why is a democratic government called 'legitimate'?
qa.a: Because it is the people's own government
qa.e: Even if slow or imperfect, a democratic government has the people's support, so it is legitimate.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why democracy is considered better than other forms of government?
qa.a: It guarantees that decisions are taken very quickly
qa.e: Democracy does not promise speed; its strengths are equality, dignity, better decisions, conflict resolution and room to correct mistakes.

qa.q: What does democracy do, according to the textbook view of outcomes?
qa.a: It creates conditions for achieving goals, which citizens must use
qa.e: Democracy is a form of government that creates conditions; citizens have to take advantage of them.

qa.q: Which practice helps make a democratic government accountable?
qa.a: Regular, free and fair elections
qa.e: Elections let citizens reward or remove governments, making them answerable to the people.

qa.q: What does 'democracy provides room to correct mistakes' mean?
qa.a: Wrong decisions can be discussed publicly and changed
qa.e: Public debate, a free press and elections allow mistakes to be noticed and corrected.

qa.q: What do studies show about economic growth in dictatorships compared to democracies?
qa.a: Dictatorships grow slightly faster, but the difference is negligible
qa.e: The difference in growth rates is very small, so democracy cannot be blamed for slow growth.

qa.q: Which of these does economic development of a country NOT mainly depend on, according to the chapter?
qa.a: The colour of the national flag
qa.e: Development depends on population size, the global situation, cooperation from other countries and economic priorities.

qa.q: Why is democracy still preferred even if its growth rate is slightly lower?
qa.a: Because it has many other positive outcomes like dignity, freedom and accountability
qa.e: Democracy is valued for much more than growth alone.

qa.q: What is 'political equality' in a democracy?
qa.a: Every adult citizen has one vote with equal value
qa.e: Each adult citizen's vote counts the same; this is political equality.

qa.q: Which statement about economic inequality in democracies is correct?
qa.a: A small number of ultra-rich people enjoy a large share of wealth, while those at the bottom have very little
qa.e: Democracies have not been very successful in reducing economic inequality.

qa.q: Why might one expect democracies to work hard to reduce poverty?
qa.a: Because the poor are a large part of the voters
qa.e: Since the poor are a large share of the electorate, no party would want to lose their votes.

qa.q: Which outcome can democracy NOT be said to have guaranteed so far?
qa.a: An end to economic inequality
qa.e: Democracies have regular elections and legitimate governments, but economic inequality persists.

qa.q: A student says, 'Democracy is useless because growth in my country is slow.' What is the best response?
qa.a: Growth depends on many factors besides the type of government, and democracy has other important outcomes
qa.e: Slow growth may be due to many factors; democracy should be judged on all its outcomes.

qa.q: Which condition is necessary for democracy to accommodate social diversity?
qa.a: Rule by majority must not become rule by the majority community in terms of religion, race or language
qa.e: Democracy requires that majority rule is not the permanent rule of one community.

qa.q: What does 'democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion' mean?
qa.a: Majority and minority opinions need to work together
qa.e: The majority must work with the minority so that the government represents general views.

qa.q: Which country is the textbook example of successfully negotiating differences among social groups?
qa.a: Belgium
qa.e: Belgium accommodated its language communities through power sharing.

qa.q: How has democracy affected the struggle of women for equal treatment?
qa.a: It accepts in principle that women are equal, so their struggle has legal and moral support
qa.e: Because democracy accepts equality in principle, women's demands for equal treatment gain support.

qa.q: What has democracy done for disadvantaged and discriminated castes in India?
qa.a: Strengthened their claims for equal status and equal opportunity
qa.e: Democracy has given these groups a stronger basis to claim equal status and opportunity, though inequalities remain.

qa.q: What does it show when people in a democracy complain about their government?
qa.a: That people are aware and can look critically at those in power — a sign of democracy's success
qa.e: Complaints show that people have become aware citizens who expect a lot from democracy.

qa.q: In which area is democracy considered far better than any other form of government?
qa.a: Promoting the dignity and freedom of the individual
qa.e: Democracy's clear strength is respect for individual dignity and freedom.

qa.q: Why should anyone be able to become part of the majority at some point in a democracy?
qa.a: So that no group is permanently excluded from power because of its birth
qa.e: If a group could never be in the majority because of its religion, language or caste, democracy would stop being fair to it.
